source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note); Lowell Offering wording verified against the Project Gutenberg text
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the market revolution transformed the American economy in the period 1800-1848.

documents.title: Fulton's steamboat on the Hudson
documents.source: Robert Fulton's Clermont, demonstrated on the Hudson River, 1807, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A description of the first successful American steamboat, written after its 1807 run from New York to Albany.
documents.text: In 1807 Robert Fulton's steamboat Clermont traveled up the Hudson River from New York to Albany by steam power, against the current, on a timetable. Within twenty years, steamboats dominated commercial shipping on the rivers and canals of the United States.

documents.title: The Tariff of 1816
documents.sourcing: The tariff Congress passed after the War of 1812, when British goods flowed back into American ports.
documents.text: Congress placed a 25 percent duty on imported manufactured goods. The duty was meant to protect young American manufacturers, whose factories had grown while British goods were cut off during the embargo and the war.

documents.title: The Erie Canal opens
documents.source: Account of the Erie Canal's completion, 1825, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A description of the canal New York State built between the Hudson River and the Great Lakes.
documents.text: The Erie Canal, completed in 1825, joined the Hudson River to the Great Lakes and New York City to the interior. Moving a ton of freight from Buffalo to New York City cost about 90 percent less after the canal opened, and New York became the nation's commercial capital.

documents.title: McCormick's reaper
documents.source: Account of Cyrus McCormick's reaper, 1831, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A description of the harvesting machine McCormick developed for grain farmers.
documents.text: Cyrus McCormick's automatic reaper, developed in 1831, cut wheat and other grains and laid them in swaths. Operated by one farmer and pulled by horses, it could harvest as much wheat as five men, and it was used on the farms of the Old Northwest.

documents.title: Mill women defend their work
documents.source: Dignity of Labor, The Lowell Offering, 1842, abridged. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An essay by the young women working in the Lowell textile mills, defending wage labor.
documents.text: "From whence originated the idea, that it was derogatory to a lady's dignity, or a blot upon the female character, to labor? . . . To be able to earn one's own living by laboring with the hands, should be reckoned among female accomplishments."

documents.title: The first telegraph message
documents.source: Samuel Morse, first telegraph message, May 24, 1844. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The first message sent on the telegraph line from Washington, D.C., to Baltimore.
documents.text: Samuel Morse sent the first telegraph message in 1844: "What hath God wrought?" By 1850, telegraph lines, usually built alongside railroad tracks, connected the country, and a clothing maker in Massachusetts could send orders to Southern cotton growers in minutes.

documents.title: The steel plow
documents.source: Account of John Deere's steel plow, 1837, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A description of the plow Deere developed for prairie farming.
documents.text: John Deere's steel plow, developed in 1837, proved more durable and efficient than the cast-iron plow. It cut through the thick prairie soil that broke older plows, and it helped open the farms of the West to commercial grain growing.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the market revolution transformed the American economy, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the cutoff of British imports during the Embargo and the War of 1812, or the growth of a national market after 1815.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including documents that show the limits of the change.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as the Panic of 1819, the Tariff of 1816, or the Waltham-Lowell system.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing where the market revolution transformed the economy and where older ways persisted.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The market revolution transformed the American economy to a great extent: it replaced local self-sufficiency with a national market tied by canals, steam, and wire, but farming still employed most Americans, and the South's cotton wealth still rested on enslaved labor.
Context: The Embargo Act of 1807 and the War of 1812 cut off British manufactured goods, forcing Americans to make their own. After 1815, peace, pride, and new machines carried that start into a full transformation.
Grouping: Documents 1, 3, and 6 show transport and communication tying the country together; Documents 2, 4, and 7 show new manufacturing and farm machines; Document 5 shows the new wage labor that ran the mills.
Beyond the documents: The cotton gin of 1793 and the growth of cotton to 58 percent of exports by 1860 tied the South's enslaved labor to Northern mills; the Panic of 1819 showed how a connected market could crash together.
Complexity: The change was deep but uneven: the North industrialized on wage labor while the South grew richer on enslaved labor, so one market held two labor systems.
